On the morning the sea went quiet, Mara was repairing a kettle.

Its whistle had been failing for months. It produced, instead of a shriek, a small embarrassed sigh. The owner, a man who wore his coat indoors, had asked her to make it sound as it had when his wife was alive.

“I can repair the whistle,” Mara had said. “I can’t promise the rest.”

Now she stood at her bench with the little brass fitting between her fingers. Through the open window she could see the water beyond the railway line, flat and blue as painted tin. It took her a while to notice what was wrong.

She looked up because she could hear the clock.

Normally, the sea covered the clock’s ticking, even here, three streets back from the shore. It covered conversations too, and dogs barking, and the groan of the early train. Mara had lived beside it for forty years and had never thought of it as loud. Only when it stopped did she understand how much it had been saying.

She went down to the beach. The waves were still coming in. They curled and broke around the stones, sending foam up toward her boots, but she heard nothing from them. A gull cried overhead. Somewhere a car door slammed.

At the waterline, a little boy was clapping at the sea, waiting for an answer.

Mara crouched beside him.

“Has it been like this long?” she asked.

He shrugged. “Since breakfast.”

His father stood a few yards away, holding a phone to his ear. “No,” he was saying, “I can see it moving. That’s what I’m telling you.”

By noon, the town had assembled at the shore. People took videos. Someone from the radio station came with a microphone and then seemed unsure what to do with it. A woman put her face in the water and came up laughing, though she wouldn’t say why.

Mara went back to her shop. On the way, she passed the bakery, where two customers were arguing over whether the silence had a cause. One blamed the shipping lanes. The other blamed the council.

She took a clean jar from her cupboard and carried it to the beach. She held it beneath a breaking wave, sealed it underwater, and brought it home.

The water inside sloshed when she tilted the jar. She could hear that. She set the jar on her bench and listened for a long time, but the water did nothing else.

That evening the man came for his kettle. Mara had forgotten it on the bench, its whistle still in pieces. She apologized and told him she would finish it in the morning.

He looked toward the shore. “I heard about that.”

“Have you been down?”

He shook his head. “I can hear the neighbors through the wall now. They play cards on Thursdays.” He paused. “I didn’t know.”

She offered him the loan of a kettle from the back room, but he said he had a saucepan.

The sea stayed quiet for six days.

People slept badly at first. Then they began to hear things they hadn’t before: the loose cover on a drain outside the post office, the harbor gate swinging in the wind, music from a house high on the hill. The man next door to Mara knocked on her wall one night to ask if she could hear his pipes. She could, and on Saturday she helped him fix them.

On the seventh morning, she woke before dawn to a slow, familiar rush. She sat up and listened. Another wave broke, and another.

She went to the window. In the dim light, she could just make out two figures on the beach. One bent down, perhaps to pick up a stone. The other waited beside them.

At nine, Mara opened the shop. The man arrived for his kettle and stood while she filled it and put it on the stove. When it boiled, the whistle came out clear and sharp. He smiled, then asked if she could make it a little quieter.

She adjusted it while he waited.
